business_problem: NVIDIA needed AI tooling that could autonomously handle complex engineering sessions and full machine-learning research workflows, not just short coding assists, while respecting privacy and infrastructure constraints.
solution_summary: NVIDIA uses Codex with GPT-5.5 as a default tool for complex engineering work and end-to-end machine-learning research. In software delivery, Codex can sustain long sessions with multiple compactions, choose the right tools or skills, and evolve internal systems from MVP to production-ready services with better scalability and reliability than earlier models. Engineers have used it to build and autonomously test a podcast-recording app in hours, including video and audio workflows via the Codex desktop app. In research, the same model acts as a creative partner: teams point it at large corpora of papers, let it trace evidence chains, map knowledge graphs, write experimental scripts, and run workloads remotely through SSH on machine-learning infrastructure. That combination means Codex can move from idea generation to experiment execution and system implementation in one flow, including rewriting legacy Python repositories into far more efficient Rust when performance improvements justify it.

data_flow: Engineering tickets, internal platform code, and research corpora are fed into Codex, which reasons with GPT-5.5 to propose designs, generate code, run tests, and launch remote experiments through SSH. Outputs are then reviewed or executed on NVIDIA’s infrastructure as production systems or ML research runs.
business_outcome: NVIDIA accelerated both software delivery and ML experimentation, lowered the threshold for building internal tools, and gave researchers a more autonomous partner for exploring ideas, tracing evidence, and launching end-to-end studies.
